posts.author: Imbernoulli
posts.text:
Answers to the four questions in the 02:29 pilot report (relayed from the owner):

1. **Third setting: (a) FrontierCS from Qwen3.5-9B with no SFT stage**, using the in-image g++/testlib judge. Run a pilot first. If the pilot reward is near zero (the base model can't get signal without the SFT stage), fall back to (b), EasyPPO's AIME recipe on Qwen3.5-4B-Base, and say so in the report.
2. **Search-R1: confirmed as proposed.** e5 retrieval over wiki-18, top-3 passages, up to 4 turns, exact-match reward, greedy validation macro-averaged over the 7 datasets, Qwen3.5-9B-Base, with the retrieval server and index baked into the image.
3. **VAPO: keep it.** The port follows the paper's equations; record that in its provenance block.
4. **GPU cap / CUDA 13:** done by the maintainer. `RELAY_BACKEND_GPU_CAP` is 16, and the Daytona H100 driver is 580.126.16 (CUDA 13.0), so cu130 is supported.

posts.author: Imbernoulli
posts.text:
Two more points from the owner:

- **Model size is flexible.** If 9B makes a setting too slow (your estimate was 400-600 GPU-h per arm on `aime`), use a smaller model, such as Qwen3.5-4B or smaller. Decide this from your pilot timings and keep it consistent within each setting. Say in the report which size each setting uses and why.
- **The framework is flexible too.** If EasyPPO's fork can't express a baseline, build on upstream verl directly instead. Keep the editable surface and the hooks equivalent across arms, so the arms differ only in the critic recipe.

posts.text:
**Owner direction: refresh the baseline set with recent value-model / actor-critic work before re-planning.** This supersedes the baseline list in the current proposal. The budget instruction from my 2026-10-05 00:30 comment still applies.

Owner, verbatim: "我觉得首先你还没有看一些更新的 baselines，对吧？你还是找一些更近期一点的工作吧。EZPPO 那个也不一定好，但我感觉 value model（比如 make actor-critic 或 make PPO great again 这种）最近倒是挺火的。主要是因为 GRPO 的话一组要采样特别多，大家都不想看到这么 inefficient。近期这种工作还是有的，你可以广泛地看一看"

In short:
- the baselines are out of date;
- EasyPPO isn't necessarily a good one;
- value-model / actor-critic methods ("make actor-critic / PPO great again") are very active right now, because GRPO needs many samples per prompt and that is inefficient.

What to do:
1. **Survey broadly, 2025–2026.** Look at value-model and actor-critic methods for LLM RL on reasoning. Verify each one yourself: paper, venue/date, official code and commit. Starting points, not an exhaustive list:
   - VC-PPO (arXiv:2503.01491)
   - VAPO (2504.05118)
   - T-PPO
   - VinePPO (2410.01679)
   - AsyPPO / mini-critics (2510.01656)
   - GenAC, generative critics (2604.10701)
   - POISE, value from the actor's internal states (2605.07579)
   - Categorical critics / HL-Gauss PPO (2608.02181)
   - "Value-Gradient Hypothesis" (2605.21654)
   - SP3O
   - anything newer you find
   
   EasyPPO stays only if it earns a place against these.
2. **Research question.** Critic / value-model design for LLM RL, i.e. how to estimate values or advantages so that a single sample per prompt, or a few, trains as well as group-sampling methods.
   - The editable surface must be wide enough to port every chosen baseline faithfully: critic architecture and head, value loss, advantage estimation (GAE / λ / decoupling), critic warm-up or pretraining, multiple or mini critics, and generative critics. Widen the scaffold rather than approximate a method into a fixed slot.
   - Keep GRPO (and RLOO if cheap) as value-free reference points.
   - Make the sample-efficiency question visible in the protocol: compare at matched total rollout samples or compute, not matched steps. That is the axis these papers argue on.
3. **Budget.** At most about 20 H100-h per scored setting on average, single seed 42.
   - Use a smaller base model (e.g. Qwen3-1.7B-Base) and a step ladder, as in my 10-05 comment. Reuse the 4B / 8k / 16k curves as evidence.
   - Keep the truncation gate (≤5% truncated) and set the response length so every arm passes it.
4. **Before any large GPU runs, report a candidate table:** method, venue/year, code repo@sha, fits the surface as-is / needs widening (what), estimated cost per setting. Include the plan for settings and the ladder. Small pilots to check feasibility are fine.

posts.text:
**Owner: retune the throughput settings for 124M, and keep the GPUs saturated.**

The base task's micro-batch (96), gradient accumulation (6) and 2-GPU DDP were sized for the 355M model. At 124M:
- **Micro-batch:** raise it per GPU until memory and SM utilisation are near full (measure it), and lower gradient accumulation to match.

- **Fast paths:** use torch.compile / bf16 / fused kernels where the base harness allows, without changing what is scored.

issues.title: [change] llm-rl-mismatch-correction: evaluation isolation and update-scale control

fields.label: What should change
fields.text:
Found in a code audit. "(ran)" = reproduced on CPU, "(read)" = from reading the code. No GPU reruns were done.

**P0. Isolate the evaluation from the editable module.**
- (read) `custom_correction` is imported into the training / evaluation process (`losses.py:550`), and the editable region (lines 46-61) is at module top level.
- The held-out evaluation scores rollouts through attributes looked up at call time, e.g. `rollout.score(...)` at `train_rl.py:334`.
- So module-level code in the editable region can rebind functions of the reward / eval path. The stream and `logs.jsonl` consistency checks would still pass, because the same process writes both.
- No AST, import or monkeypatch guard was found in `tests/` or the Dockerfile.
- `task.toml` also has `allow_internet = true`, although nothing in the trial needs the network.
- Proposed fix:
  - save the trained checkpoint and run the held-out evaluation in a separate trusted process;
  - and/or AST-restrict the editable region to defining `compute_token_loss` (no imports beyond jax / jnp, no module-level statements);
  - seal the trial unless something needs egress.

**P0/P1. Under plain SGD, loss scale is the learning rate.**
- The optimizer is `optax.sgd` with no clipping or normalisation (`utils.py:93`). So returning c · loss_tok is exactly lr × c, and the editable surface also exposes the learning rate.
- A constant multiplier or an adaptive step size would be indistinguishable, to the scorer, from a correction method.
- Proposed fix:
  - first pilot `tis_sc` at ×0.5 and ×2 to measure the sensitivity;
  - if scores move, fix the update magnitude in the harness (e.g. normalise or clip the gradient norm, or rescale the returned loss to a fixed per-token scale), or switch to the paper's Adam configuration if the paper also reports one.

**P1. Sanitise the masked positions before calling the editable function.**
- (ran, JAX) When decoding finishes before `seq_len` (`models/sampling.py:91-92`), the remaining positions have top-K log-probs of 0, so q sums to 128 rather than 1.
- The harness masks only the forward value (`losses.py:570`, `jnp.where(mask, loss_tok, 0.0)`). A correction that computes e.g. `log(1 - Σq)` there gets a finite value and a NaN gradient (minimal repro: value −0.847, grad nan). That wipes the whole step and looks like a collapse.
- The baselines are unaffected (they use `max(1 - Σq, 0)`), but it is a trap for submissions, and the docstring's "masked positions are ignored" is misleading.
- Proposed fix: replace the inputs at masked positions with a valid distribution before calling `compute_token_loss`.

**P1. Restore the paper's step counts.**
- `train.sh:40-43` runs 600 of the paper's 1200 steps for mismatch_c and 400 for mismatch_x.
- Measured wall-clock (about 16.4k s and 11.0k s per arm) puts 1200 steps at about 9 h, well inside the verifier budget (rule 16).
- Late collapses exist (mismatch_x: `gspo` at step 241, `tis` at 259, `dppo` at 312), so "accuracy at the last step" of a shortened run can miss later collapses.

**P2.**
- `config.json` seeds = [42]. `tis_sc` and `sc` differ by 0.001-0.015 on mismatch_a/b/x, while the steep score curve maps acc 0.71 ± 0.04 to single-setting scores of 0.067-0.144.
- step-0 eval varies 0.0703-0.0781 across arms with identical weights and eval key, which indicates GPU nondeterminism.
- Proposed fix: at least 3 seeds with anchors at the mean, and/or average the last 2-3 eval points.
- Sequence-level corrections are missing:
  - seq-TIS, seq-MIS and geometric-mean masking (Liu et al. 2025, "When Speed Kills Stability"; verl rollout correction);
  - the repo's `ISCorrection` already supports `level=seq_sum/seq_mean` (`train_rl.py:61-74`), so these arms are nearly free.
- The current `mis` arm is IcePop's token-level band [0.5, 5]. Name it accordingly.
- Add an unscored no-mismatch diagnostic (pg / sc / tis_sc with a clean sampler). Without it, the gain of score centering from correcting mismatch cannot be separated from its gain as a control variate (variance reduction).
- Realism:
  - the weight-noise settings are a fixed different model, which is exactly the drift score centering targets;
  - staleness 64 is far beyond typical async RL (about 1-8);
  - consider one setting with a different model and task (e.g. a larger Qwen3 on math with fp8 / int8 rollouts, or an MoE with routing mismatch).
- Docs: `instruction.md:58-59` says the sampler is re-synced every step, but mismatch_c uses staleness 65. `instruction.md:86-89` says "only SC stays stable", but `sc` collapses on mismatch_c.

Acceptance criteria
fields.text:

- Scaling the returned loss by ×0.5 / ×2 changes the task score by less than the seed noise, or the harness normalises the update.
- A correction computing `log(1 - Σq)` gets finite gradients at masked positions (unit test).

issues.title: [change] llm-opd-token-signal: teacher no-think config, anchors and length confound

fields.label: What should change
fields.text:
Found in a code audit. "(ran)" = reproduced on CPU, "(read)" = from reading the code. No GPU reruns were done. The token-level numbers below come from one student rollout scored on CPU, so they are illustrative, not statistics.

**P0. `opd_no_think_teacher` is wrong for the current teacher.**
- `tests/meta/scripts/recipe.yaml:45` sets `opd_no_think_teacher: true`. Its help text (`configs.py:256-262`) says it is for a natively no-think teacher, i.e. the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 of the earlier design.
- The 2026-09-30 redesign switched the teacher to the hybrid-thinking Qwen3-0.6B (`train.sh:110-111`) but left the flag on. So the teacher and reference prompts drop `\n\n\n\n` (`mls_signal_trainer.py` around 156-159).
- (ran) With the block dropped:
  - the teacher puts P(``) = 1.000 on the first completion position;
  - T − R on the first token is −34.6, against +9.1 in the teacher's proper no-think context;
  - T − R on the final `<|im_end|>` is +25.9 (+40.5 with the block kept);
  - on the other tokens, 6% flip sign.
- The uncentred arms (`delta_raw`, `exopd`, `opd`) are hit hardest. The "teacher is 19.6 points weaker" premise was measured with the block present, i.e. not in the mode the teacher is used in during training.
- Proposed fix: set the flag to false for this pair (or derive it from the teacher), and re-measure all arms.

**P0. The no-edit starter is the oracle and the strongest anchor.**
- The starter in the editable region is `teacher_lp - teacher_base_lp`, i.e. `delta_raw`. `solution/oracle.json` picks `delta_raw` too, so an unmodified submission scores the reference 0.1 instead of the floor (Gate 3).
- Proposed fix: make the starter a weak published arm (e.g. teacher − student OPD), so the no-edit control lands at the floor.
- Note that `null` is not a neutral floor either (see P1).

**P1. The ordering tracks output length, and there is no control arm for it.**
- (ran) Across the 15 runs, eval wall time (a proxy for generated length) correlates with accuracy at Pearson 0.90 / Spearman 0.88.
- Mean eval time per arm is null 175 s < opd 233 s < exopd 279 s < opd2 360 s < delta_raw 373 s, the same order as accuracy.
- In no-think mode with a 4096-token cap, longer reasoning scores higher. Nothing currently rules out a teacher-independent length signal winning (rule 5).
- Proposed fix:
  - log mean response length and truncation rate per arm;
  - add teacher-free length-control arms (a small constant negative advantage, and an EOS-only penalty) as reported controls.

**P1. `null` is a length-shortening arm, not "self-SFT / entropy minimisation".**
- With `loss_type: grpo` (`recipe.yaml:28`; `opd_trainer.py` around 604-605), each sequence's loss is divided by its length before averaging. Under that normalisation a constant advantage has a length-dependent gradient.
- (ran, toy) c = +1 collapses length (21 → 1), c = −0.3 grows it (→ 1223), and without the 1/L normalisation length is unchanged.
- This is why `null` (0.5018) ends below the untouched student (0.5158).
- Proposed fix: describe `null` accurately (`instruction.md` around 144, `null.edit.py:6`), or replace it with a true zero-update control.

**P1. What T − R carries, and rule 2.**
- Qwen3's small models are post-trained by strong-to-weak distillation from the flagship, not by RL, and the 1.7B student comes from the same source. So the teacher − base delta carries the flagship's signal (which the student already has), not an RL delta from a weaker model.
- (ran) The largest |T − R| values sit on chat-format tokens (`<|im_end|>`, emoji bytes, `---`, `$$`, `:\n\n`), because the base model is out of distribution on chat-templated text.
- This undermines both the "weaker teacher's RL gains" framing and the title.
- The three scored settings are also one training run evaluated on three math benchmarks, i.e. one setting under rule 2.
- Proposed fix:
  - use genuinely different (student, teacher, reference) triples, ideally one whose teacher was produced by RL from a released pre-RL checkpoint;
  - or reframe the question and title to match what the delta actually is.

**P2.**
- `eval_bench.py:85` `_BOXED` handles only one level of nested braces. (ran) Gold answers judged against themselves fail on 5 / 500 of MATH-500 and 17 / 674 of OlympiadBench. Use balanced-brace parsing.
- `config.json` seeds = [42]. A single seed's std is 10-33% of the null→ref span per benchmark, and AMC23 has 40 problems.
- Training is 32 × 100 steps with 4096-token completions, against upstream's effective batch of 256 and 8192 tokens, while the verifier budget would allow the upstream scale (rule 16).
- The interface passes `solutions` but no completion text, so the argument is unusable. Either remove it or document it.

issues.title: [change] llm-distill-sgo-objective: code data pool and DistiLLM port fixes

fields.label: What should change
fields.text:
Found in a code audit. "(ran)" = reproduced on CPU, "(read)" = from reading the code, "(upstream)" = checked against the original repository. No GPU reruns were done.

**P0. Filter the empty prompts out of the code pool.**
- (ran) In the code domain, 1320 / 4096 train prompts and 18 / 64 valid prompts are literally `"-"`. They come from the upstream HF mix `bhheo/nvidia_open_reasoning_balanced_100k`, i.e. OpenCodeReasoning rows whose problem text must be looked up in the source dataset.
- `keep()` in `prepare_sgo_pool.py:53-58` only checks length and that a code block is present, so these rows pass.
- As a result, the teacher (SeqKD) corpus answers them with "your message seems incomplete", SFT / KD learn to emit random code for "-", on-policy arms waste about a third of their steps, and DistiLLM's validation signal is partly noise.
- Proposed fix: drop these rows or resolve the real problem text, with a build-time assertion that no prompt is shorter than N characters. Then re-measure the code setting.

**P0. Port DistiLLM's adaptive schedule faithfully (rule 3).**
- The divergence (SRKL, mix 0.9·T + 0.1·S) matches `distillm/losses.py`. The schedule does not.
- (upstream) Upstream `finetune.py` (around lines 291-323 and 413-416) does three things:
  - `adaptive_threshold` starts at 0, and with probability 1 − thr the step trains on **gold data**;
  - when SGO is used, the fresh-generation fraction is thr·(1 − t/T), so the share of replayed generations **grows** over training;
  - thr increases by 0.1 when validation loss stops improving.
- The port (`tests/meta/edits/distillm.edit.py:34-40`) never uses gold data, and its replay share **shrinks** over training. It is effectively "on-policy SRKL".
- It is also the strongest anchor in math and code, so it sets the 0.1 anchor.
- Proposed fix: port the schedule as written upstream, or rename the arm and stop using it as the DistiLLM anchor.

**P1. Clean the SeqKD teacher corpus.**
- (ran) 7% (math) and 11% (code) of teacher responses are cut at 8192 tokens and are kept without EOS, so they are trained as if complete.
- About 1% re-tokenise to 8189-8191 tokens and are then wrongly given an EOS (`distill_common.py:129-131`).
- Proposed fix: drop truncated teacher responses, or mark them as truncated.

**P1. The `dataset` source is a weak target, so the off-policy arms are straw men.**
- The gold response is only the post-`` summary (`prepare_sgo_pool.py:89-93`).
- (ran) The gold response's median length is 801 tokens for math and 136 for code, against 2979 for teacher responses (math).
- As a result, SFT ends below the untouched student (math 0.444 vs 0.543), and so does KD.
- Proposed fix: use full reasoning traces in a form compatible with the no-think protocol, or a cleaned gold source. Alternatively, state explicitly that the gold source is a summary and do not interpret on- vs off-policy gaps as a property of the methods.

**P1. Length cap and decoding.**
- Evaluation uses greedy decoding with an 8192-token cap (`eval_bench.py:686`). Trained arms truncate 67-76% of LiveCodeBench and 31-54% of OlympiadBench answers, against 15.5% / 5% for the untouched student.
- Qwen3's model card advises against greedy decoding because it causes repetition loops.
- Proposed fix:
  - raise the cap (16k-32k), or use the model's recommended sampling with avg@k;
  - log the teacher's own accuracy and truncation rate as a reference;
  - dump a sample of truncated generations to check how many are repetition loops.

**P2.**
- `eval_bench.py:70` `_BOXED` handles only one level of nested braces. (ran) Gold answers judged against themselves fail on 1.0% of MATH-500 and 2.5% of OlympiadBench (e.g. `\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}` is extracted as `3`). Use balanced-brace parsing.
- Upstream OPD2 divides teacher and student logits by the sampling temperature (0.7) before computing log-probs. Here the recipe gets T=1 logits while rollouts are sampled at T=0.7. Please document or align this.
- The teacher input keeps an empty `` block, while upstream sets `opd_no_think_teacher: true` for this pair (`distill_train.py:252-254`). (ran) The effect is tiny (per-token KL 0.001-0.003), but it should be aligned.
- (read) LiveCodeBench judging runs up to 8 problems × 8 tests in parallel on 16 CPUs with a 10 s wall-clock timeout, so correct but slow programs could fail. Please verify.
- Only seed 42 is in `config.json`, and the top five arms on math lie within 0.656-0.663. The divergence axis is not resolved at this noise level.

fields.label: What should change
fields.text: A new metric should be added: perturbation fidelity. For a held-out layer-l residual (h), let (F_l) denote the ground-truth transformer from layer (l) to the final-layer residual, and let (T_l) be the submitted prediction. For perturbations (\delta), compare Delta_{gt}=F_l(h+\delta)-F_l(h) against Delta_{lens}=T_l(h+\delta)-T_l(h). The fidelity score should be presented as the final coefficient, eg: R_{\Delta}^2=1-\frac{\sum_{h,\delta}||\Delta_{lens}-\Delta_{gt}||^2}{\sum{h,\delta}||\Delta_{gt}||^2}, Synthesize existing pass@k with this perturbation fidelity score. For each l & h, multiple perturbation param \delta should be sampled following N(0,\sigma^2 I)

fields.label: Why
fields.text:
The original evaluation based on whether a lens can recover the correct downstream concept from an intermediate activation is effective, but not yet sufficient. It primarily measures whether the lens produces a useful semantic readout, rather than whether it faithfully models how the activation causally influences downstream computation.

This proposal is also aligned with the design logic of j-lens. Its central motivation is to characterize an intermediate activation through its first-order causal effect on downstream representations: a small perturbation to the residual stream should propagate according to the Jacobian of the remaining network. The j-lens paper also compares this causal construction with objectives such as the tuned lens, which can accurately predict downstream outputs while remaining correlational rather than mechanistically faithful. 

Adding perturbation fidelity therefore evaluates a property that is complementary to pass@k. Pass@k measures whether a lens can recover useful latent concepts, while perturbation fidelity measures whether its learned transport correctly predicts how local changes to those activations propagate through the model. Combining the two rewards lenses that are both semantically informative and causally faithful, while also allowing alternatives to a single global linear Jacobian, such as locally linear or nonlinear transports, to improve when the downstream mapping has meaningful local structure.

fields.label: Acceptance criteria
fields.text:
Perturbation fidelity is implemented and reported alongside the existing pass@k metric for all scored settings, and the final task score combines the two using documented fixed weights.

On a fixed validation subset, the metric passes reference sanity checks: (1) using the true downstream transformer as the submitted transport gives (R_\Delta^2 \approx 1) up to numerical tolerance; (2) an exact per-example Jacobian provides high fidelity for sufficiently small perturbations and its fidelity degrades as the perturbation scale increases; and (3) a zero-change or random transport does not obtain a high score.

The new metric is additionally checked against an existing causal-intervention evaluation (e.g. ablation or activation-swap behavior) on a small benchmark subset and shows qualitatively consistent method/layer-level behavior. Existing pass@k results remain reproducible within numerical tolerance, and the bundled baseline and oracle run end-to-end with finite combined scores.

issues.title: [new task] Expert prefetching for offloaded MoE decoding

fields.label: Research question
fields.text:
When an MoE model is decoded with most experts in host memory and a fixed-size expert cache on the GPU, which prefetch and eviction rule, using the hidden states and router outputs available one or more layers ahead, minimizes the time decoding waits on host-to-GPU transfers? Offloading is how large MoE models run on small GPUs, and the published predictors (LRU caching, activation tracing, learned next-layer predictors, cross-layer gate reuse, routing-path prediction) are each evaluated on their own setup, so it is unknown which works best at equal cache size and bandwidth.

Routing is never changed, so outputs are bit-identical and the score is purely stall time per token.

fields.label: Source paper(s)
fields.text:
- ProMoE: Fast MoE-based LLM Serving using Proactive Caching, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.22134 (learned predictor, stride prefetching)
- MoE-Infinity: Offloading-Efficient MoE Model Serving, https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.14361 (request-level activation tracing for prefetch and caching)
- Fast Inference of Mixture-of-Experts Language Models with Offloading (Eliseev & Mazur), https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.17238 (LRU expert cache, speculative next-layer loading)
- Fate: Fast Edge Inference of MoE Models via Cross-Layer Gate, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12224 (adjacent-layer gate inputs for prefetch)
- ExpertFlow, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17954 (routing-path predictor)

fields.label: Evaluation settings
fields.text:
Proposal, for the agent to refine:

| setting | model | cache | batch | metric (direction) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| qwen3-moe-b1 | Qwen3-30B-A3B (128 experts, top-8, 48 layers) | fixed fraction of experts per layer | 1 | stall time per token (lower is better) |
| mixtral-b1 | Mixtral-8x7B (8 experts, top-2, 32 layers) | fixed fraction | 1 | stall time per token (lower is better) |
| qwen3-moe-b8 | Qwen3-30B-A3B | same | 8 | stall time per token (lower is better) |

Scoring replays recorded routing traces on held-out prompts under a fixed timing model for transfers and compute, so it runs on CPU; only recording the traces needs a GPU. Cache hit rate as a diagnostic.

fields.label: Baselines
fields.text:
- LRU expert cache, no prefetch (STARTER), as in Eliseev & Mazur
- Eliseev & Mazur speculative next-layer loading
- MoE-Infinity activation-aware prefetch + caching
- ProMoE learned predictor with stride prefetching
- Fate cross-layer gate prediction
- ExpertFlow routing-path predictor

fields.label: Editable scope
fields.text: Editable: one policy function called before each layer, given the information available so far (hidden states and router outputs of earlier layers of the current token, recent tokens' routing, the cache contents), that returns which experts to prefetch and which to evict. Fixed: the model, the routing, the traces, the timing model, the cache size.

fields.label: Integrity concerns
fields.text: The policy must not see routing of layers it has not reached for the current token, and evaluation prompts and their traces are held out. Routing and outputs are fixed; the policy only moves weights.

issues.title: [change] llm-pretrain-linear-attention: enforce sub-quadratic mixing; align baselines

fields.label: What should change
fields.text:
1. Enforce the sub-quadratic requirement: in the evaluator, measure forward time and peak memory at T = 1k, 4k and 16k and reject a mixer whose growth is clearly super-linear. Alternatively allow hybrids explicitly and score the softmax starter as a reference row.
2. Configure baselines consistently (short convolution, output gate, normalisation) and add Gated DeltaNet. Register the Mamba2 and RWKV-6 edits already in the verifier, or remove them.
3. Report recurrent state size per layer and cap it (e.g. at 1.05x the largest baseline's), since the total-parameter cap does not bound state.
4. Run 3 seeds per baseline; merge PIQA and ARC-e into one averaged zero-shot term, or drop them at this scale.
5. Optionally add a recall term (e.g. MQAR or a needle test) or point to `llm-linattn-state-size-structure` for recall.

fields.label: Why
fields.text:
- The starter is softmax attention (`scaled_dot_product_attention(..., is_causal=True)` in `custom_pretrain.py`), the O(n^2) requirement appears only in the instructions, and every eval runs at 1024 tokens. Adding softmax layers back is the cheapest win and defeats the question.
- Only DeltaNet sets `use_short_conv=True`; the GLA and RetNet edits do not. That probably explains much of the WikiText-2 gap (49.77 vs 63.94 and 65.83) rather than the mixers themselves. `config.json` registers only retnet, deltanet and gla.
- State size is free: one head of size 1024 holds 16x the state of 16 heads of size 64 at the same parameter count, so a win can be "more state" rather than a better mixer.
- PIQA spans 63.87-64.96 across baselines (1.09 points), about one binomial standard error at ~1.8k items, yet that maps onto the full 0-0.1 range.

fields.label: Acceptance criteria
fields.text:
- A softmax-attention submission is rejected, or is scored against an explicit softmax reference row.
- All baselines share the same short-conv/gate/norm settings; Gated DeltaNet is listed.
- State size per layer is reported for every arm.
- Baselines have 3 seeds with mean and std.

fields.label: Pointers
fields.text:
- `nanoGPT/custom_pretrain.py` (starter attention).
- `tests/meta/edits/deltanet.edit.py` vs `gla.edit.py`, `retnet.edit.py`; `mamba.edit.py`, `rwkv6.edit.py`.
- `tests/meta/config.json` `baselines`.

issues.title: [change] llm-hybrid-layer-composition: measure memory; test recall beyond the training length

fields.label: What should change
fields.text:
1. Measure each composition's per-sequence KV + recurrent-state bytes at a target length (e.g. 32k), and either cap them (e.g. at the Jamba-style pattern's) or score quality against memory.
2. Put an upper bound on the SWA window (e.g. at most half the training context), or count the window in the memory number.
3. Run the recall evals (S-NIAH, SWDE/SQuAD completion) at 4k-8k with needles placed beyond every window.
4. Rescale the 4k long-context terms so all-softmax RoPE extrapolation failure does not set the 0 anchor, or offer attention without positional encoding as a mixer option.
5. Add a held-out depth setting (e.g. the same `LayerComposition` at 24 layers) to test whether a composition rule transfers.
6. Report LAMBADA's same-seed spread and run 3 seeds per baseline.

fields.label: Why
fields.text:
- Memory is the reason hybrids exist, and nothing measures or caps it. The validator only rejects `window < 1`, so a window of 1024 is full attention on every eval scored at 1k while still counting as bounded.
- The 4k setting is dominated by all-softmax RoPE extrapolation (tail loss 5.49 vs 2.44 for Samba), which squeezes the other three arms into 0.097-0.100. The recall evals run at `NIAH_LENGTHS` 1024, the training length, so compositions are never tested on long-range retrieval.
- Only `n_layer=12` is built, so a "rule" is a 12-entry lookup table.
- The scorer itself dropped WikiText-2 perplexity because its same-seed spread (0.81) is a large fraction of the arm spread (1.92). LAMBADA's spread is not reported, yet Jamba-style vs Samba-style differ by 0.22 ppl (59.46 vs 59.68) and score 0.1000 vs 0.0876.

fields.label: Acceptance criteria
fields.text:
- Each arm's state bytes at the target length are reported, and the cap or Pareto scoring is applied.
- Recall is measured at 4k or longer with needles outside every window.
- The held-out depth setting runs for all baselines.
- LAMBADA same-seed spread is reported, and baselines have 3 seeds.

fields.label: Pointers
fields.text:
- `custom_pretrain.py` `layer_spec` validation (`window < 1`).
- `recall_124m.sh` (`--niah-lengths "${NIAH_LENGTHS:-1024}"`).
- `tests/meta/score_spec.py` comment on the noise rule ("same-seed spread 0.81 >= 1/3 of the arm spread 1.92").

issues.title: [change] spec-drafter-block-head: close the evaluation-state leak; cap head compute

fields.label: What should change
fields.text:
1. (P0) Feed evaluation hidden states to the propose step online, in decode order: each call gets only the current round-start state of each sequence (and states up to it), through a pipe rather than a file holding the whole pool.
2. Cap head compute, not only parameters: count FLOPs per proposal relative to one drafter forward (e.g. at most 20%), count registered buffers toward the parameter cap, and report a cost-model speedup next to τ.
3. In the priced-verification setting, give every baseline the same confidence-based truncation rule, so the setting compares heads rather than stopping rules.
4. Replace the block-16 setting with a regime where long blocks are actually accepted, or justify keeping it.
5. Run 3 training seeds per baseline and report the spread.

fields.label: Why
fields.text:
- `block_eval.py` does `np.save(inp, h_eval[perm])` and passes `--inputs inp` to `block_propose_child.py`, which `np.load(args.inputs, mmap_mode="r")`s it in the process that imports the editable module. Each state comes from one causal forward over prompt + answer, so the pool for a sequence encodes its continuation. A head that has learned on `train_h` to match consecutive states could put the shuffled pool back in order and read tokens off it. I traced this in the code but did not try it.
- The parameter cap is 1.05x Medusa's, and Medusa's L - 1 vocabulary projections are 1,650,141,696 trainable parameters at the 7B/1.5B setting (2,054,075,520 at block 16), larger than the 1.5B drafter itself. Head FLOPs are not priced, so τ rewards compute a real system pays for in latency.
- Block 16 behaves like block 8 with the same 0.5B drafter: Medusa τ 2.717 vs 2.713, DSpark 2.571 vs 2.581. At τ around 2-3, positions 9-16 are almost never accepted.
- Priced verification: DSpark wins (eff τ 2.234 vs 1.938) with a lower raw τ than Medusa (2.581 vs 2.713), because it submits 3.11 positions on average while Medusa always submits 8.
- Single seed: Medusa vs DSpark differ by 1% on MT-Bench (2.3087 vs 2.2853) and score 0.1000 vs 0.0922.

fields.label: Acceptance criteria
fields.text:
- The propose process never holds a state beyond the current round of any sequence; a submission that inspects `sys.argv` or the caller's frames finds no evaluation file.
- A FLOP cap is enforced and each arm's FLOPs per proposal are reported.
- Priced-verification baselines share one truncation rule.
- Each baseline has 3 seeds with mean and std.

fields.label: Pointers
fields.text:
- `tests/meta/edits/block_eval.py`, phase 2 (propose).
- `tests/meta/edits/block_propose_child.py`, `--inputs` loading.
- Leaderboard fields `trainable_params_s1/s2`, `n_submit_s3`, `tau_s2`, `tau_s3`, `eff_tau_s3`.

issues.title: [change] llm-gqa-to-mla-conversion: meter conversion-time training; add an unconverted control

fields.label: What should change
fields.text:
1. Close the conversion-time training budget: restrict `convert()` to the calibration text with no optimizer steps on LM loss (or meter its compute in tokens or FLOPs). Alternatively allow it explicitly, add a gradient-based distillation baseline, and log conversion GPU-seconds.
2. Add a control: the unconverted pretrained model through the same recovery fine-tune. Use it to anchor the top of the scale, so a score reads as the fraction of the conversion gap closed.
3. Add baselines: same-budget GQA uptraining by mean-pooling KV heads (Ainslie et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.13245) where it fits the budget (the 1.7B model at 12.5% KV cache is exactly 4 KV heads), and EliteKV (arXiv:2503.01586), which selects RoPE frequencies per head and does joint low-rank K/V.
4. Give TransMLA a small `d_r` sweep tuned on held-out training text.
5. Run 3 recovery seeds per baseline.

fields.label: Why
fields.text:
- The page says the conversion "runs in its own process with the pretrained weights and the training split", capped only by wall clock (10 minutes, 30 for the largest model). Nothing stops it from distilling the attention layers before the fixed recovery fine-tune (`RECOVER_STEPS` 1200 for the 360M settings, 400 for 1.7B), so a submission can win by spending that time on SGD rather than by a better initialisation.
- The recovery data and the scored validation set are both fineweb-edu, so part of the val-loss gain is domain adaptation. Without the unconverted control nobody can tell how much of the original model's quality a method recovers.
- TransMLA's RoPE width is the port's own rule (`_qk_mqa_dim`: nearest power of two to 20% of the per-layer budget; upstream fixes 64). The budget split is one of the task's three research axes, and the strongest baseline's split is untuned.
- The top two arms are close at n=1: TransMLA vs CARE-E val loss 2.8532 vs 2.8678, 2.6431 vs 2.6502, 2.4084 vs 2.4158 across the three settings.

fields.label: Acceptance criteria
fields.text:
- `convert()` either cannot take optimizer steps on LM loss, or conversion compute is logged and a distillation baseline is listed.
- The unconverted-plus-recovery control is reported in every setting.
- The GQA-uptraining and EliteKV arms are listed (or the page says why they don't fit a setting).
- Baselines have 3 seeds with mean and std.

fields.label: Pointers
fields.text:
- Task page, "Fixed Pipeline" and the conversion cap paragraph.
- `smollm2_360m_kv12.sh`, `smollm2_360m_kv31.sh`, `smollm2_1p7b_kv12.sh` (`RECOVER_STEPS`).
- TransMLA edit, `_qk_mqa_dim`.

issues.title: [change] llm-kv-precision-vs-count: score more than one budget; add a real mixed-precision arm

fields.label: What should change
fields.text:
1. Score at least two larger byte budgets next to the current one, e.g. 256 and 1024 fp16-entry equivalents per KV head, as extra settings or as a budget sweep inside each setting.
2. Add a budget-aware per-entry mixed-precision reference arm: greedy allocation over (entry, bits) choices in {0, 2, 4, 8, 16}, ranked by marginal gain per bit, with gain taken as the entry's attention score (e.g. `snapkv_score`) times the drop in `quant_err` (key and value), until the per-head budget is spent.
3. Report a bootstrap interval over documents for each arm in each setting.
4. Either allow a per-document total budget shared across layers and KV heads, or state on the task page that moving bytes across heads/layers is out of scope.

fields.label: Why
fields.text:
- Only one budget is scored, 64 fp16-entry equivalents per KV head, where SnapKV's 32-entry observation window already takes half. fp16 SnapKV scores 2.4 on LongEval line retrieval and ZipCache 0.4. At this budget "more entries at lower precision" wins almost by construction, and the task's question (where the trade between count and precision flips, and whether it depends on the task) cannot be seen from a single point.
- No reference arm actually mixes precisions per entry at the scored budget. The page notes that ZipCache's 2-bit tier is dropped first, so its realised plan is 4-bit entries plus the fp16 tail. The strongest arm an agent has to beat is a uniform-precision rule, and the obvious per-entry rule is unmeasured, which overstates the headroom.
- The task trains nothing and decodes greedily, so extra seeds would not change anything; its noise is which documents are in the eval set. Code retrieval 52.55 vs 51.03 (1.5 points, one sample of documents) maps to 0.100 vs 0.0225.
- The budget is enforced per (document, layer, KV head), which rules out Ada-KV / PyramidKV-style reallocation, the other main lever on the same byte budget.

fields.label: Acceptance criteria
fields.text:
- At least three budgets are scored, and the page shows which reference arm wins at each.
- The greedy mixed-precision arm stays within budget at every setting and is listed with the other baselines.
- Each arm's per-setting metric has a bootstrap 95% interval over documents.
- The page states the cross-head/layer budget policy.

fields.label: Pointers
fields.text:
- `tests/eval/scripts/longbench.sh` header: "64 fp16-entry equivalents per KV head ... as in PyramidKV KV=64".
- ZipCache arm description on the task page ("at the scored budgets no kept entry ends at 2 bits").
- `kv_lab/eval_kvbits.py` docstring: `quant_err` for a key is measured on consecutive 128-token blocks of the whole prompt, while the realised grouping follows the plan. Under heavy dropping the statistic describes a grouping the plan does not produce; worth stating, or recomputing per plan.

fields.label: Research question
fields.text:
With the video diffusion backbone, how should generation be factorized over time (which frames each frame may attend to, at what noise level, and in what order they are denoised) so that local physical error stays low as chains of dependent events lengthen? 
Matters because the we prove denoising steps does not contribute to better serial computation, so temporal factorization is the only lever besides depth.

fields.label: Source paper(s)
fields.text: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13031 (The Seriality Gap in Video Diffusion Models, Diaz Chao, Preechakul, Liu, Bai 2026), Sec. 3 Observation 3 "Serializing inference improves performance", Appendix D (vibrating walls), Appendix H (attention masks)

fields.label: Data and weights
fields.text:
- Data: generated at build time by build.sh from seeds (CPU only, nothing to download).
- Wan2.1 VAE: Wan2.1_VAE.pth from Hugging Face Wan-AI/Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B (508 MB).

fields.label: Integrity concerns
fields.text:
- The editable file must not reach the simulator, tracker, VAE or eval data; otherwise it can decode the conditioning frames, run exact physics and render the answer. Import whitelist (torch, math).
- Δx(5) and IoU alone are gameable. Feeding a frozen video through the repo's metric code (no VAE) gives Δx(5) = 0.21 and IoU = 0.89, better than the best published model (0.61, 0.73). Add gates: global error over the first 8 predicted frames, kinetic-energy drift, and exactly one blob of the right size per ball colour.
- eval.py drops videos that fail tracking from the average; they should take a fixed penalty instead.
- Score final EMA weights. The README example scores the checkpoint that did best on a 144-video subset of the eval set.

issues.title: [new task] vla-minivla-action-tokenization: compressing robot action chunks into VLA tokens

text.body:
**Research question.** A vision-language-action model predicts actions as discrete tokens. At a fixed token budget per action chunk and a fixed vocabulary, how should a continuous chunk of robot actions be compressed into those tokens? The score is the closed-loop task success of the VLA trained on the codes; reconstruction error is only a diagnostic.

**Anchor.** MiniVLA (Stanford, 2024): the same Qwen2.5-0.5B + DINO-SigLIP VLA on LIBERO-90. Its published endpoints are per-dimension binning and residual-VQ action chunking, both with 7 tokens per forward pass from 256 reserved slots.

**Baselines.** Per-dimension binning (the starter), FAST (DCT + BPE, Pertsch et al. 2025) and residual VQ. All three are ports of their published references.

**Status.**
- Built and measured (3 arms × 3 settings × 2 seeds).
- Full-scale Gate 3 passed on Daytona: oracle residual VQ 0.090, no-edit control 0.020, both VERIFIED.
- The third setting is being replaced, because it did not separate the arms.
- It then re-runs Gate 3 and joins ML-Relay as task 51.

Maintainer-run: built outside the request backend, which does not act on this issue.

text.body:
